claims.text: A trace Nb addition introduced during alloy synthesis preferentially segregates to lamellar colony boundaries.
Nb segregation reinforces lamellar colony boundaries.
Reinforcement of colony boundaries delays microcrack initiation and propagation.
Trace Nb addition will simultaneously improve yield strength and room-temperature tensile ductility.
The target eutectic high-entropy alloys have a dual-phase lamellar microstructure with numerous internal boundaries.
Weak interlamellar interfaces trigger microcrack initiation during room-temperature tensile deformation.
Controlled solidification and post-solidification heat treatment can facilitate selective Nb segregation to colony boundaries.
A thin Nb-enriched interfacial layer forms along lamellar colony boundaries.
Nb segregation increases the cohesive strength of weak colony interfaces.
Increasing interfacial cohesive strength reduces local stress concentrations that cause microcrack formation.
Boundary-segregated Nb does not impede dislocation motion within the lamellae.
Preserving dislocation motion while strengthening interfaces reconciles the strength–ductility trade-off.
The Nb-modified alloy will have higher yield strength than the unmodified lamellar-colony baseline.
The Nb-modified alloy will have higher ultimate tensile strength than the unmodified lamellar-colony baseline.
The Nb-modified alloy will have greater room-temperature elongation at failure than the unmodified lamellar-colony baseline.
The beneficial effects require Nb to remain at trace levels and to segregate selectively without forming deleterious secondary phases.
Exceeding the unspecified Nb or processing thresholds may cause embrittlement.
The magnitude of the strength and ductility improvements depends on Nb concentration and processing conditions.
